docs.title: Trano
docs.text:
Trano

Trano is an innovative Python package that automates the creation of complex Building Energy Simulation (BES) Modelica models from simplified information contained in widely used data formats like YAML, JSON, or RDF. Unlike traditional tools that directly convert BIM to BES, Trano introduces an intermediate step, paving the way for seamless integration with IFC translators.

Trano is Modelica library agnostic but is natively designed to work with: ✅ Validated detailed Modelica libraries (e.g., Buildings, IDEAS,...) ✅ Reduced-order models (e.g., AIXLIB, ISO13790,...) ✅ Models for optimal control (FastModel: close to Buildings, closed loop or for optimal control, translated to CasADi) ✅ your library...

docs.text:

The HVAC components (radiators, valves, pumps, boilers, heat pumps, air handling units) come from the Buildings library for every Modelica library. The Modelica name of every parameter in every library is listed in the parameter reference.

The models trano generates are validated against ASHRAE Standard 140 (BESTEST): the 27 single-zone cases are simulated for a year with every library and compared with the acceptance limits of the standard and the spread of the reference programs. Buildings and IDEAS pass every case (see the validation results and the walk through the cases); the two simplified zones are reported for information. Simulations run in the official OpenModelica image.

docs.title: Graphviz
docs.text:
Trano employs Graphviz to arrange various Modelica components within the model. While installation is not mandatory, it is advisable for enhanced model visualization. You can install Graphviz by following the instructions on the official website. For Windows installations, ensure the Graphviz bin folder is added to the system PATH.

To install Graphviz on Linux, use the following command:

sudo apt-get install graphviz

sudo apt update
sudo apt install graphviz

docs.title: Docker
docs.text: Trano utilizes the official OpenModelica Docker image to execute simulations. It is recommended to install Docker on your system so that Trano can pull the required images and run simulations. You can install Docker by following the instructions on the official website.

docs.title: Modelica libraries
docs.text:
The simulation container installs the Modelica libraries Trano generates models for: Buildings 13.0.0 (built against Modelica 4.1.0), IDEAS 3.0.0 and AixLib 3.0.1 (both built against Modelica 4.0.0), on the openmodelica/openmodelica:v1.26.9-ompython image. Both Modelica Standard Library versions are installed side by side; the versions are defined in one place, trano_simulate.ModelicaEnvironment. IDEAS 4.0.0 is not used yet: no OpenModelica release handles it (1.25 cannot parse it, 1.26 and 1.27 fail with internal errors on its weather bus, also in IDEAS' own examples).

Each simulation container first runs an OpenModelica script that installs these libraries with the package manager. A library already present on the container's MODELICAPATH (for example baked into an image derived from the official one under /root/.openmodelica/libraries) is not installed again, so simulations also work where the package index cannot be reached.

Without further configuration, the libraries are installed at every container start, which needs network access. Two ways avoid it:

  • mount a directory of installed libraries into every simulation container by setting the environment variable TRANO_MODELICA_LIBRARIES to it;
  • install the libraries once, when an image is built, with the omc of that image: python -m trano_simulate.install_libraries runs the same installation as a container start and exits with a non-zero status when Modelica, Buildings, IDEAS or AixLib is still missing afterwards.
FROM openmodelica/openmodelica:v1.26.9-ompython
RUN pip install trano && python -m trano_simulate.install_libraries
ENV TRANO_SIMULATION_RUNTIME=local

docs.title: Simulation runtimes
docs.text:
Trano runs OpenModelica in one of two ways, chosen by the runtime argument of trano_simulate.simulate or, by default, by the environment variable TRANO_SIMULATION_RUNTIME:

  • docker (the default): a sibling container of the OpenModelica image is started through the Docker socket for every simulation, with a unique name, and the libraries are installed in it as described above;
  • local: the omc found on the PATH runs in the process' machine, for example in a worker container built as above. Nothing is installed at run time; trano.exceptions.OpenModelicaNotFoundError is raised when omc is missing.

In both cases the model, its script and its weather file are written into the project directory and the result file lands in its results directory. Two simulations must not share a project directory.

The one-call API validates, generates and simulates a model and returns a typed result instead of raising:

from pathlib import Path

from trano import simulate_yaml
from trano_simulate.simulate import SimulationOptions

result = simulate_yaml(
    Path("house.yaml"),  # or the model already parsed into a dict
    options=SimulationOptions(end_time=7 * 24 * 3600),
    runtime="local",
    on_phase=print,  # generating, compiling, simulating, done
)
if result.success:
    print(result.result_path)
else:
    print(result.error_kind, result.error_message)  # validation, translation, solver, timeout or runtime

trano.check_yaml checks the model with OpenModelica without simulating it, and trano.kpi.building_kpis(result.result_path, network) computes the heating energy, peak power and hours below the set point of models heated by ideal_heating_cooling emissions.

docs.title: Python package
docs.text:
Warning

Trano requires python 3.9 or higher and docker to be installed on the system.

Trano is a Python package that you can install via pip.

pip install trano

Trano can also be utilized with Poetry.

poetry add trano

The Python package enables the generation of a Modelica model from the YAML configuration input. However, to simulate the model, Docker must be installed on the system.

On Windows systems, you may need to enable long path support. Refer to the Microsoft documentation for guidance.

docs.title: Check installation
docs.text:
To verify the installation, execute the following command in the terminal.

trano verify

This command checks your system's compatibility for model generation and simulation. Compatibility is optional if you only intend to generate the Modelica model.

docs.title: FastModel
docs.text:
FastModel is the trano library of fast models close to Buildings: from the same YAML file as Buildings and IDEAS, it generates a model whose physics follow Buildings.ThermalZones.Detailed.MixedAir and the Buildings hydronic and ventilation components, written so that rumoca translates it into a CasADi ODE \(\dot x = f(t, x, u, p)\). The same model simulates in OpenModelica and in CasADi, where trano_optimization estimates its state and solves optimal control problems with IPOPT.

The library comes in two configurations of the same components and templates:

  • FastModel, the closed loop: the controllers of the YAML (thermostatic valves, pump, three-way valve, boiler and heat pump controls, ideal heating and cooling) are part of the model, written without events, and the water flows follow the pressures of the circuits. Its only inputs are the weather and the internal gains: it simulates the building as the Buildings and IDEAS models do;
  • FastModelMPC, for optimal control: the controllers are left out and the controls of the systems are inputs of the model, which the optimisation decides; the flows are set by the valves.
trano create-model house.yaml FastModel       # closed loop: house.mo with building_mpc and its runnable building
trano simulate-model house.yaml FastModel     # simulates building with OpenModelica
trano create-model house.yaml FastModelMPC    # the model for optimal control, its controls as inputs

This page describes the components of the library and their equations, what the library does not model, and how close and how fast it is, ending with the most complex YAML file it simulates compared with Buildings and IDEAS. The FastModel tutorial shows how to use the model in CasADi.

FastModel before the closed loop

Until the closed loop was added, FastModel was the model for optimal control. That model is now FastModelMPC: code that builds an optimal control problem with Library.from_configuration("FastModel") takes Library.from_configuration("FastModelMPC").

docs.title: How a model is built
docs.text:
FastModel is used as trano uses Buildings and IDEAS: a Modelica library, trano/library/FastModel.mo, and one template per element of the YAML file, trano/elements/library/models/fast_model/*.yaml. The library is embedded in every generated package; the constructions and glazings of the YAML are written as records of its Data package. The generated package holds two models:

  • building_mpc, the building: an explicit ODE whose inputs are the weather data and the internal gains, and, with FastModelMPC, the controls of the systems. It holds no table, no event and no component of another library: this is the model rumoca translates;
  • building, the runnable model: building_mpc fed with the weather file (the Buildings reader, which also gives building_mpc the location of the site), the occupancy schedules and the external data of the network: with FastModelMPC, the controls replayed from it (each held at 1 without data); with FastModel, the set points of the MonitoredSetpoint emission controls.

Walls, windows and floors are elements of their own connected to the bus of their zone, as in IDEAS. The templates render each system in the mode of the library (library in the templates): with FastModel, each controller of the YAML is a component of FastModel.Controls connected to the system it drives, and every water component is pressure-driven (pressureDriven=true); with FastModelMPC, each controllable system declares its control as a top-level input of building_mpc named <element>_y (bounded to 0..1) or <element>_Q (a heat flow rate, bounded by the nominal power), and the controllers are not rendered: their decisions are the inputs.

docs.title: Rules for an explicit ODE
docs.text:
Every component keeps a few rules, so that the assembled model translates into \(\dot x = f(t, x, u, p)\):

  • every node joined by connections has a heat capacity, or is solved in closed form inside its component (the radiant star of a room, the mixing of water flows);
  • the equations are smooth (once continuously differentiable): power laws, maxima and table interpolations are regularised, conditions are inside functions or noEvent;
  • water flows are set (FastModelMPC): each valve sets the flow of its branch, a mixing valve the share of supply water, mass balances the rest; the production (boiler, heat pump) or the ventilation unit closes the balance of its circuit, one per circuit. Or they are pressure-driven (FastModel): each component has a pressure node of small compliance at its inlet, so that the pressures are states and every flow an explicit function of them (see water circuits);
  • controllers have no event (FastModel): hysteresis is a fast bistable state, limits are smooth, PI controllers have anti-windup and a smooth reset;
  • a port with several connections is an array, one element per connection, sized by the template: the inlets of a component mix, its outlets leave at its outlet temperature;
  • parameters computed by functions (the conductance of a radiator, the polynomial fits of the window optics, the scaling of the heat pump tables) take values settled at translation.

docs.title: Components and equations
docs.text: The notation: \(T\) temperatures [K], \(Q\) heat flow rates [W], \(\dot m\) mass flow rates [kg/s], \(A\) areas, \(c_p\) the specific heat capacity of water (4184 J/(kg.K)) or of air (1006 J/(kg.K)), \(\rho\) densities (1000 and 1.2 kg/m3), \(\sigma\) the Stefan-Boltzmann constant.

docs.title: Smooth functions
docs.text:
The library replaces the non-differentiable functions of Buildings by the regularised ones of Buildings.Utilities.Math.Functions:

  • regStep(x, y1, y2, ε): a cubic step from \(y_2\) (\(x < -\varepsilon\)) to \(y_1\) (\(x > \varepsilon\)); smoothMax, smoothMin and smoothLimit are built on it;
  • positivePart(x, δ) \(= \tfrac12\left(x + \sqrt{x^2 + \delta^2}\right)\), a smooth \(\max(x, 0)\);
  • the natural convection law \(Q = A\,c\,|\Delta T|^{4/3}\) is written \(Q = A\,c(\Delta T)\,\Delta T\,(\Delta T^2 + \Delta T_0^2)^{1/6}\), with \(\Delta T_0 = 0.1\) K and the coefficient \(c\) blended smoothly between its values for a surface warmer or colder than the air.

docs.title: Weather and solar irradiance
docs.text:
BoundaryConditions.Weather takes the seven channels of a weather file or a forecast (TDryBul, TBlaSky, winSpe, winDir, HDirNor, HDifHor, HGloHor) and computes the solar position from the model time, as Buildings.BoundaryConditions.SolarGeometry:

\[ \delta = \arcsin\!\left(-\sin 23.45^\circ \cos\frac{2\pi (t/86400 + 10)}{365.25}\right), \qquad t_{sol} = t - t_{zone} + \frac{\lambda\,43200}{\pi} + E(t), \qquad \omega = \frac{2\pi}{24}\left(\frac{t_{sol}}{3600} - 12\right) \] \[ \cos\theta_z = \cos\varphi \cos\delta \cos\omega + \sin\varphi \sin\delta \]

with \(E\) the equation of time, \(\varphi\) the latitude and \(\lambda\) the longitude, and the Perez coefficients \(F_1\), \(F_2\) of the diffuse sky from the sky clearness and brightness (the eight clearness bins joined by smooth steps). BoundaryConditions.TiltedSurface gives the irradiance on a surface of tilt \(\beta\) and azimuth \(\gamma\):

\[ H_{dir} = \max(\cos\theta\, H_{dir,nor}, 0), \qquad H_{dif} = H_{dif,hor}\left[(1 - F_1)\frac{1 + \cos\beta}{2} + F_1 \frac{\max(0, \cos\theta)}{\max(\cos 85^\circ, \cos\theta_z)} + F_2 \sin\beta\right] + H_{glo,hor}\,\rho_g\frac{1 - \cos\beta}{2} \]

where \(\theta\) is the incidence angle on the surface and \(\rho_g = 0.2\) the ground reflectance. The site (latitude, longitude, time zone) comes from the weather file in building; in building_mpc it is a parameter.

docs.title: Opaque surfaces
docs.text:
Envelope.OuterWall, BoundaryWall, AdiabaticWall and InternalWall conduct heat through the layers of their construction, with a node at each layer boundary (\(n\) layers, \(n + 1\) nodes). The capacity of a node is half of each adjacent layer, the conductance of a layer \(k/x\):

\[ C_j = A\left(\tfrac12 x_{j-1}\rho_{j-1} c_{j-1} + \tfrac12 x_j \rho_j c_j\right), \qquad G_j = \frac{A\,k_j}{x_j} \] \[ C_1 \dot T_1 = Q_{sol} - Q_{ext} - G_1 (T_1 - T_2), \qquad C_j \dot T_j = G_{j-1}(T_{j-1} - T_j) - G_j (T_j - T_{j+1}), \qquad C_{n+1} \dot T_{n+1} = G_n (T_n - T_{n+1}) - Q_{int} + Q_{rad} \]
  • Outer surface (OuterWall): absorbed sun \(Q_{sol} = \alpha_{sol} A (H_{dir} + H_{dif})\); exchange with the outside \(Q_{ext}\) as Buildings.HeatTransfer.Convection.Exterior (TemperatureWind) and SkyRadiationExchange: natural convection, forced convection \(h_F = 2.537\, W R \sqrt{P v / A}\) for a square surface (\(P = 4\sqrt A\)), with \(W\) = 1 windward, 0.5 leeward and 0.75 without wind (smooth in the wind direction and speed) and \(R = 1.67\) for a rough surface, and the long-wave exchange with sky and ground linearised around their mean radiant temperature \(T_{env} = \left(F_{sky} T_{sky}^4 + (1 - F_{sky}) T_{out}^4\right)^{1/4}\), \(F_{sky} = (\pi - \beta)/\pi\): \(Q_{lw} = 4\sigma\varepsilon A T_{env}^3 (T_1 - T_{env})\).
  • Floor on ground (BoundaryWall): the outer surface is held at the ground temperature of the YAML (10 degC by default), as trano does for Buildings' datConBou, or at the outdoor air temperature (outdoor_air variant).
  • Party wall (AdiabaticWall): no heat crosses the outer surface.
  • Wall or floor between zones (InternalWall): each face exchanges with its own zone; side b faces the other way (tilt \(\pi - \beta\), a floor seen from below is a ceiling).
  • Inner surface: natural convection to the room air \(Q_{int}\) with the coefficients of Buildings (1.3 for a wall; 0.76 or 1.51 for a ceiling or a floor depending on whether it is warmer than the air), or a fixed coefficient; long-wave and solar exchange with the room \(Q_{rad}\) (see the zone).

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
Envelope.Window models each pane of its glazing as a node, the gas gaps as conductances, and the frame as a conductance between the room air and the outside, after Buildings.HeatTransfer.Windows:

\[ C_i \dot T_i = Q_{abs,i} + G_{i-1}(T_{i-1} - T_i) - G_i (T_i - T_{i+1}) \quad (\text{outer pane: } - Q_{ext},\ \text{inner pane: } - Q_{int} + Q_{rad}) \]
  • \(G_i = A_{gla} / (R_{pane,i}/2 + R_{gap,i} + R_{pane,i+1}/2)\), the glass area \(A_{gla} = (1 - f_{fra})A\);
  • the optics of the glazing are computed by trano from its layers with the algorithm of Buildings (Buildings.HeatTransfer.Windows.Functions, after Finlayson et al.: angular properties of each pane from its normal-incidence values, panes combined by the net radiation method): direct transmittance \(\tau\) and absorptance \(a_i\) of each pane at the incidence angles 0, 10, ..., 90 degrees, and their hemispherical values; the gap resistances follow EN 673. The library fits a quartic in \(\cos\theta\) through the ten angles (least squares, at translation), so that the optics are smooth in the sun position: \(Q_{abs,i} = A_{gla}\left(H_{dir}\, a_i(\cos\theta) + H_{dif}\, a_i^{hem}\right)\);
  • transmitted radiation, distributed in the room by the zone: \(Q_{tra,dir} = A_{gla} H_{dir} \tau(\cos\theta)\), \(Q_{tra,dif} = A_{gla} H_{dif} \tau^{hem}\);
  • outside: \(Q_{ext} = A_{gla}(4 + 4v)(T_1 - T_{out}) + Q_{lw}\) (the wind-dependent film coefficient of the Buildings window model and the sky exchange above);
  • frame: \(Q_{fra} = \dfrac{f_{fra} A}{1/h_e + 1/U_{fra} + 1/h_i}\,(T_{air} - T_{out})\), taken from the room air.

docs.title: Zones
docs.text:
Zones.Zone balances the air of the room, exchanges long-wave radiation between its surfaces through a radiant star, and distributes the transmitted solar radiation, after Buildings.ThermalZones.Detailed.MixedAir:

\[ m_{sen}\,\rho c_p V\,\dot T_{air} = \sum_i Q_{con,i} + Q_{con,emitters} + A_{flo}\, q_{con} + \rho c_p V \frac{n_{ach}}{3600}(T_{out} - T_{air}) + \sum_k \dot m_k c_p (T_{sup,k} - T_{air}) \]

with \(Q_{con,i}\) the convective heat of each surface, the internal gains \(q_{con}\) per floor area, the infiltration \(n_{ach}\) (air changes per hour, infiltration variant) and the supply air of a ventilation unit (VentilatedZone; the extract air leaves at \(T_{air}\)). The long-wave exchange is linearised at \(T_0 = 20\) degC: each surface \(i\) has the conductance \(G_i = 4\sigma T_0^3 \varepsilon_i A_i\) to the radiant star, whose temperature balances the radiant gains:

\[ T_{rad} = \frac{\sum_i G_i T_i + Q_{rad,emitters} + A_{flo}\, q_{rad}}{\sum_i G_i}, \qquad Q_{rad,i} = G_i (T_{rad} - T_i) + k_{dir,i} Q_{tra,dir} + k_{dif,i} Q_{tra,dif} \]

The transmitted diffuse radiation is absorbed in proportion to \(\alpha_i A_i\) (\(k_{dif,i} = \alpha_i A_i / \sum_j (\alpha_j + \tau_j) A_j\)); the direct radiation hits the floors first, and what they reflect is spread over the other surfaces, as SolarRadiationExchange of Buildings. A radiant emitter sees the mean surface temperature \(\sum_i G_i T_i / \sum_i G_i\).

docs.title: Water circuits
docs.text:
The water ports carry a mass flow rate and the temperature of the water crossing them. A component mixes its inlets (regularised by \(\dot m_{small} = 10^{-6}\) kg/s so that a closed branch keeps a defined temperature) and its outlets leave at its outlet temperature:

\[ T_{in} = \frac{\sum_k \dot m_k T_k + \dot m_{small}\, \overline{T_k}}{\sum_k \dot m_k + \dot m_{small}} \]

Set flows (FastModelMPC):

Component Equations Valve \(\dot m = y\,\dot m_{nom}\): the valve sets the flow of its branch (control <valve>_y) ThreeWayValve (mixing) \(\dot m_1 = y\,\dot m\), \(\dot m_3 = (1 - y)\,\dot m\), \(T_2 = y T_1 + (1 - y) T_3\) (control <valve>_y) Junction, Junction2 mass balance; the outlets leave at the mixed temperature of the inlets Pump pass-through; electrical power \(P = \Delta p_{nom}\,\dot m / (\rho\,\eta)\) TemperatureSensor pass-through; \(T\) is the water temperature (no sensor dynamics)

Pressure-driven flows (FastModel, the parameter pressureDriven of every component): each component has a pressure node at its inlet, of small compliance, whose pressure \(p_{in}\) is a state; the flow of each outlet is an explicit function of \(p_{in}\) and of the pressure of the inlet node downstream, with the resistances of Buildings linearised as Buildings does (linearized=true):

\[ \tau_{hyd}\, G_{hyd}\, \dot p_{in} = \sum_{inlets} \dot m - \sum_{outlets} \dot m, \qquad \tau_{hyd} = 5\ \text{s} \] Component Flow of an outlet Valve \(\dot m = G\,(p_{in} - p_b)\), \(\dfrac{1}{G\,\dot m_{nom}} = \dfrac{\Delta p_{fix}}{\dot m_{nom}^2} + \dfrac{\Delta p_{valve}}{(\varphi(y)\,\dot m_{nom})^2}\), \(\varphi\) the equal-percentage characteristic of Buildings (rangeability \(R\), leakage \(l\)) ThreeWayValve a node per inlet; \(\dot m_1 = G_1 (p_1 - p_2)\) equal-percentage in \(y\), \(\dot m_3 = G_3 (p_3 - p_2)\) linear in \(1 - y\), the bypass \(K_v\) scaled by fraK Junction, Junction2 \(\dot m = G\,(p_{in} - p_b)\) on each outlet, \(G = \dot m_{nom} / \Delta p_{nom}\) (at least 1000 Pa) Radiator \(\dot m = \dot m_{nom}\,(p_{in} - p_b) / \Delta p_{nom}\) Boiler the quadratic law \(\dot m = \dot m_{nom}\,\Delta p / \sqrt{\Delta p_{nom}}\,(\Delta p^2 + (\delta_M^2 \Delta p_{nom})^2)^{-1/4}\), linear below \(\delta_M \dot m_{nom}\) Pump its curve (SpeedControlled_y: 1.14, 1 and 0.42 times \(\Delta p_{nom}\) at 0, 1 and 2 times \(\dot m_{nom}\)) scaled to the speed \(y\): \(\Delta p / (y^2 \Delta p_{nom}) = 1.14 + 0.08\,x - 0.22\,x^2\), \(\dot m = y\,\dot m_{nom}\,x\), the positive root; \(P = \Delta p^+ \dot m^+ / (\rho\,\eta)\) TemperatureSensor, HeatPump, pipes a small linear resistance, 1000 Pa at the nominal flow (no resistance in Buildings)

While the pressures settle, a flow may reverse for a moment: the components mix the positive parts of their inflows and carry the positive part of their flow, so that the temperatures stay finite. The circuit has no fixed pressure: the compliances hold the mass of the water, and only the pressure differences matter.

Radiator (RadiatorEN442_2 of Buildings): \(n_{ele} = 5\) water and metal elements in series, each emitting by the EN 442 power law, a share \(f_{rad}\) radiant:

\[ \frac{C}{n_{ele}}\dot T_i = \dot m c_p (T_{i-1} - T_i) - Q_{con,i} - Q_{rad,i}, \qquad Q_{con,i} = (1 - f_{rad})\, UA_{ele}\, \Delta T_i (\Delta T_i^2 + \Delta T_0^2)^{(n-1)/2} \]

with \(\Delta T_i = T_i - T_{air}\) (radiant part: \(T_i - T_{rad}\)), \(n = 1.24\), \(C = \rho V_{wat} c_p + 500\, m_{dry}\) and the water volume and dry mass of Buildings (5.8e-6 m3/W and 0.0263 kg/W of nominal power). As Buildings at initialisation, \(UA_{ele}\) is solved (by bisection, at translation) so that the radiator emits its nominal power at its nominal water and room temperatures.

Boiler (BoilerPolynomial), with set flows the reference of its circuit: the part load ratio \(y\) is the control (FastModelMPC) or comes from Controls.BoilerTemperatureControl (FastModel),

\[ Q_{fuel} = y\,\frac{Q_{nom}}{\eta_{nom}}, \qquad C\,\dot T = \dot m c_p (T_{in} - T) + \eta(y, T)\, Q_{fuel} + UA\,(T_{amb} - T), \qquad \dot E_{fuel} = Q_{fuel} \]

with the efficiency curves of Buildings (constant, polynomial in \(y\), or quadratic-linear in \(y\) and \(T\)), its water volume, dry mass and heat loss to the boiler room.

Air-to-water heat pump (AirToWaterTableData2D with the Vitocal 251-A08 data of Buildings, scaled to the capacity of the YAML) charging a mixed buffer, with set flows the reference of its circuit: the compressor speed \(y\) is the control (FastModelMPC) or comes from Controls.HeatPumpControl (FastModel),

\[ T_{con,out} = T + \Delta T_{con}\, y, \qquad Q_{con} = y\, s\, \tilde Q(T_{con,out}, T_{out}), \qquad P_{el} = y\, s\, \tilde P(T_{con,out}, T_{out}) \] \[ C\,\dot T = \dot m c_p (T_{in} - T) + Q_{con} + UA\,(T_{amb} - T), \qquad \dot E_{el} = P_{el} \]

with \(s = Q_{nom} / \tilde Q(T_{set}, T_{out,des})\) the scaling of the tables, \(\tilde Q\) and \(\tilde P\) the EN 14511 tables made differentiable (quadratic in the condenser temperature through the rows at 35, 45 and 55 degC, linear in the source temperature with the kinks smoothed over 1 K), \(C\) the buffer and the condenser water, and \(UA\) the insulation of the buffer. Its coefficient of performance at the current temperatures, \(\mathrm{COP} = \tilde Q / \tilde P\), is a variable of the model, defined also when the compressor is off.

docs.title: Ventilation
docs.text:
Ventilation.Duct carries \(\dot m = y\,\dot m_{nom}\), the speed \(y\) of the fans of its unit travelling along the ducts and through the zones. Ventilation.HeatRecoveryUnit (trano's system D: constant-effectiveness heat exchanger and two constant-pressure fans), the reference of its air loop, with the fan speed \(y\) as its control:

\[ T_{sup} = T_{out} + \varepsilon\,(T_{ext} - T_{out}) + \frac{P_{sup} + \varepsilon P_{ret}}{\dot m_{nom} c_p}, \qquad P_{fan} = y\,(P_{sup} + P_{ret}), \qquad P = \frac{\Delta p_{nom}\,\dot m_{nom}}{\rho\,\eta_{fan}} \]

where \(T_{ext}\) is the mixed extract air of the zones and the fans heat the air (the supply fan after the exchanger, the return fan before it).

docs.title: Controls (closed loop)
docs.text:
FastModel.Controls holds the controllers of trano's Buildings models, written without events so that the closed-loop model stays an explicit, smooth ODE:

  • a hysteresis (CDL Hysteresis) is a bistable state switching within \(\tau = 10\) s, \(\tau \dot y = \mathrm{regStep}\big(u - (u_{high} + (u_{low} - u_{high})\,y)\big) - y\);
  • a PI controller (Modelica LimPID) limits its output smoothly, with back-calculation anti-windup: \(y = \mathrm{lim}(k(e + I))\), \(\dot I = e/T_i + (y - y_{unl})/(k N_i T_i)\); while disabled, its integral relaxes to the reset value in 30 s;
  • the day schedules of set points ({on, off, ...} in seconds of the day) change with smooth steps of 60 s, the time of day taken without events.
Controller Equations EmissionP (emission control PController) \(y = \mathrm{lim}_{0}^{1}\big(k\,(T_{set} - T_{zon})\big)\), \(T_{set}\) the occupied or setback set point of the schedule EmissionPI (default) PI towards \(T_{set}\), \(k = 0.1\), \(T_i = 900\) s (heating loop of Buildings G36) EmissionOnOff (onoff) hysteresis on \(T_{set} - T_{zon}\), band 0.1 K EmissionMonitored (MonitoredSetpoint) P controller towards the set point input <control>_TSet, which building reads from the column of the external data named in the YAML (held at the occupied set point without data) CollectorControl the pump runs when a valve of its circuit opens beyond 0.5 and stops when all are below 0.01 (hysteresis on their smooth maximum); its speed \(y = \mathrm{lim}_0^1\big(k\,(1 - \Delta p/\Delta p_{nom})\big)\) while it runs ThreeWayValveControl \(y = \mathrm{lim}_0^1\big(k\,(T_{col,set} - T_{mea})\big)\), the supply temperature measured downstream with a 10 s lag BoilerDemand (boiler control simple) demand when a valve of its circuits opens beyond 0.5, none when all are below 0.01 BoilerTemperatureControl part load ratio \(y = d\,\mathrm{lim}_0^1\big(k\,(T_{set} - T_{boi})\big)\) with the demand \(d\) (1 without a simple boiler control) HeatPumpControl supply set point on the heating curve, from TSet at the design outdoor temperature to 30 degC at the heating limit (16 degC); heating season by a hysteresis of ±1 K at the limit; the buffer charges below the set point minus half the band dTHys until it is half the band above; the compressor PI (\(k = 0.1\), \(T_i = 300\) s, minimum speed 0.3) on the condenser outlet, towards the set point plus dTHys

docs.title: Electricity and ideal systems
docs.text:
• Electrical.Photovoltaic (PVSimpleOriented): \(P = A\, f_{act}\, \eta\, \eta_{DC/AC}\, (H_{dir} + H_{dif})\) on the plane of the modules, metered as EPro.
  • HVAC.IdealHeatingCooling (FastModelMPC): the heat flow rate \(Q\) is an input <element>_Q, split between the room air and the radiant star by its radiant share.
  • HVAC.IdealHeater (FastModel): an ideal emitter delivers \(Q = y\,Q_{nom}\), \(y\) from its emission control.
  • HVAC.IdealHeatingCoolingPI (FastModel): a PI controller per mode (\(k = 0.1\) per kelvin, \(T_i = 300\) s) towards the day tables of the heating and cooling set points, limited by the capacities, metered as EHea and ECoo.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
Not modelled: generating a model stops with a message naming the element. Boilers with a storage tank, water-to-water heat pumps, chillers, domestic hot water tanks, batteries, EV chargers, VAV boxes and their controls, air handling units other than the balanced unit with heat recovery (system_d), and power sensors.

Simplifications:

  • Controllers without events (FastModel). The controllers follow those of trano's Buildings models, but a hysteresis switches within 10 s instead of at an instant, and the safety controls of the heat pump (minimum on and off times) are not modelled: the heat pump starts and stops more often than in Buildings, which shows in the water temperatures (about 2 K RMSE) and in the hour-by-hour heat of the radiators (6–16 % CV(RMSE)), less in the zones and the meters. The boiler controls default and complex charge a storage tank, which FastModel does not model: a boiler without storage driven by them always has demand, its temperature control alone sets its firing.
  • The controls are inputs (FastModelMPC). The controllers are left out: the optimal control decides, or the runnable model replays the controls of the external data. Without data, building holds every control at 1.
  • Flows. With set flows (FastModelMPC), each valve sets the flow of its branch: the sharing of flow between branches (pump curves, valve authorities, balancing) is not computed. With pressure-driven flows (FastModel), the resistances are linearised at their nominal flows (as Buildings does with linearized=true), and the components that have none in Buildings (sensors, the condenser of the heat pump) have a small one. One production per hydraulic circuit, and mixing three-way valves only: diverting valves are not modelled.
  • Ventilation units are balanced (supply = extract) and run at constant pressure rise; infiltration is a constant air change rate (no wind- or stack-driven air flows).
  • The envelope follows Buildings, not IDEAS: the floor on ground sees a fixed ground temperature (IDEAS models the ground with ISO 13370), and overhangs and side fins of the windows are not modelled. The long-wave exchange in a room is linearised at 20 degC, the interior convection uses the natural convection laws of Buildings.
  • No moisture: sensible heat only, with constant air properties; the co2 occupancy variant only brings its heat gains.
  • The heat pump is the Vitocal 251-A08 of Buildings scaled to the capacity of the YAML, heating only, without the safety controls (minimum on and off times) of Buildings.
  • Tools: the runnable model needs OpenModelica (or Dymola) and Buildings for the weather reader; the CasADi export of the connected building_mpc, closed loop or not, needs rumoca 0.10.3 (rumoca main up to c74cddf, 2026-10-13: the later commits stop the export of these models at residual_equations). The closed-loop model exports too, but its fast controllers and pressure nodes make it stiff: CVODES takes about 100 s per simulated day for the renovated house, where OpenModelica runs its four weeks in under two minutes.

docs.title: Accuracy
docs.text:
The validation simulates the Buildings (or IDEAS) model of a YAML file with its own controls and compares it with FastModel in two ways: the closed-loop FastModel with its own controllers, and the FastModelMPC model replaying the controls of Buildings (the heat of the ideal emitters, or the flow of each radiator branch, the position of each three-way valve, the boiler part load ratio or the heat pump speed and the fan speed; everything else is simulated by FastModel). Zone air temperature RMSE per case:

Case Zones Systems Closed loop (FastModel) Replay (FastModelMPC) BESTEST 600FF / 900FF (a year) 1 free floating 0.39 K / 0.33 K 0.39 K / 0.33 K BESTEST 600 / 900 (a year) 1 ideal heating and cooling 0.06 K / 0.14 K 0.65 K / 0.41 K Three zones (January) 3 ideal heaters, walls between zones 0.06–0.11 K 0.18–0.49 K Heat pump house (January) 6 heat pump, buffer, radiators 0.15–0.25 K 0.15–0.33 K Residential house before renovation (January) 6 gas boiler, radiators 0.05–0.11 K 0.12–0.20 K Residential house after renovation (January) 6 heat pump, buffer, three-way valve, radiators, ventilation with heat recovery, PV 0.06–0.14 K 0.12–0.17 K

In closed loop the controllers correct the small differences of the envelope as the Buildings controllers do, where the replayed controls are open loop: the zones follow Buildings more closely. The meters follow within a few percent (closed loop: fuel +1.2 %, heat pump electricity −1.1 and −3.1 %, fans −2.1 %, PV 0.0 %; replay: fuel +0.0 %, heat pump electricity −1.6 and −1.8 %, fans −0.6 %). The radiators deliver the heat of Buildings within 0.7–4.3 % CV(RMSE) hour by hour in the replay, 2–16 % in closed loop, where the heat pump starts and stops at other instants than in Buildings (it has no minimum on and off times). Against IDEAS, on the renovated house, the zones stay within 0.14–0.23 K in closed loop and 0.31–0.39 K in the replay (see the showcase below).

docs.text: The showcase below times the most complex YAML file FastModel simulates in OpenModelica and in CasADi, against Buildings and IDEAS.

docs.title: Showcase: a renovated house with every system
docs.text:
examples/residential_after_renovation.yaml is the most complex YAML file FastModel simulates: the Belgian semi-detached house of the residential reference cases after a deep renovation, with every kind of system the library models.

Zones 6 (living room, kitchen, three bedrooms, bathroom), 110.6 m2, on two storeys Envelope 15 external walls and roofs, 10 windows (triple glazing), 2 slabs on ground, 3 party walls, 10 walls and floors between zones Heating air-to-water heat pump of 3 kW with a 100 l buffer, pump, mixing three-way valve, split valve, 6 radiators with their valves Ventilation balanced unit with 80 % heat recovery, 12 supply and extract ducts Electricity 4.2 kWp PV array building_mpc (FastModelMPC) 189 states, 28 inputs (9 controls, 7 weather channels, 12 internal gains), 2807 parameters

The house is simulated for the four weeks of January in Uccle by Buildings and by IDEAS, each with its own controls (thermostatic valves, heating curve and safety controls of the heat pump, three-way valve control). The closed-loop FastModel runs the same house with its own controllers. FastModelMPC then replays the controls of each library: the flow of each radiator branch, the position of the three-way valve, the compressor speed and the fan speed. The heat pump, the buffer, the water circuit, the radiators, the ventilation unit, the PV and the six zones are simulated by FastModel.

python -m validation.mpc compare residential_after --models FastModel FastModelClosedLoop --references Buildings IDEAS
python -m validation.mpc.benchmark residential_after

docs.title: Speed
docs.text:
Four weeks of January, OpenModelica 1.26.9 (DASSL, tolerance 1e-6), on the same 4-core machine:

Model Translation and compilation [s] Simulation [s] Buildings 182 886 IDEAS 167 373 FastModel (building, replaying the controls) 24 99 FastModel closed loop (building, its own controllers)* 10 105 FastModelMPC in CasADi (building_mpc, CVODES, inputs held over 5-minute steps) 30 (rumoca) 9

* Measured later on another 4-core machine, where the replay simulates in 84 s: the closed loop costs about a quarter more than the replay.

FastModel simulates the four weeks 9 times faster than Buildings and 4 times faster than IDEAS in OpenModelica, and about 100 times faster than Buildings once translated to CasADi. The Buildings and IDEAS runs record the signals the replay needs every minute, the FastModel run every 15 minutes.

The CasADi model is the same model as the OpenModelica one: simulated with the inputs of the OpenModelica run, its zone temperatures stay within 0.014 K of it over the four weeks.

Optimal control. A day-ahead problem of the house (hourly steps, the 9 controls, comfort at 20 degC from 7 to 22 h and 17 degC otherwise, electricity bought at 0.30 and sold at 0.05 per kWh) is solved by IPOPT from the middle of January:

Radau collocation points per hour (CollocationSettings.degree) NLP variables IPOPT iterations Solve time [s] 1 about 9 600 100 39 2 about 14 200 97 117 3 (default) about 18 700 165 380–475

The model itself costs little (about 2 s of evaluations in the slowest solve): the time goes into the factorisations of the KKT system, whose Hessian blocks couple the 189 states at every collocation point. For a model of this size, fewer collocation points per step, or a shorter horizon, keep the solve within a minute.

docs.title: Component variants
docs.text:
Most components in Trano (radiators, spaces, controls, air handling units, boilers, valves, ...) ship with several pre-defined implementations called variants. A variant is a concrete Modelica realisation of a component class — for example the Radiator class has a default variant (RadiatorEN442_2, a water radiator), an ideal variant (an idealised heat injection block driven by its control) and an idealbus variant (the same, driven through the data bus).

This tutorial explains:

  1. What variants are and where they live in the codebase.
  2. How to use an existing variant from your YAML model.
  3. How to create a new variant (built-in or in your own folder).
  4. How to register an external variants folder so Trano picks up your variants automatically.
  5. How variants interact with model validation.
  6. How to test custom variants.

docs.title: 1. What is a variant?
docs.text:
A variant describes how an instance of a Trano element class (e.g. Radiator, Space, EmissionControl, AirHandlingUnit, ...) is rendered to Modelica code.

Each variant is a YAML entry that contains:

Field Purpose classes The Trano element class(es) this variant applies to (e.g. Radiator). variant The string name used to select this variant from a YAML model. library The library (or list of libraries) this variant targets (default, ideas, buildings, FastModel, ...). template The Jinja2 template rendered into the generated Modelica model. ports Connection ports the component exposes (fluid, heat, data, weather). parameter_processing How the user-provided parameters are mapped to the template. figures Plots auto-generated for the reporting view (optional). component_template An optional inner Modelica model wrapping the component (optional).

The built-in variants live under trano/elements/library/models/<library>/<component>.yaml. Each YAML file contains a list of variant definitions for one or several classes. A definition whose library is default serves every library that has no definition of its own for that class and variant.

docs.title: Examples of variants currently shipped
docs.text:
The table below summarises the variants that already exist for the most common components, so you can pick the right one for your model. The full list can always be discovered with:

from trano.elements.library.components import get_components_registry

for c in get_components_registry().components:
    print(c["classes"], c["variant"], c.get("library"))

PController Proportional (P) controller. MonitoredSetpoint P controller whose setpoint is read from a data source (e.g. measured boundary data).

docs.title: 2. Selecting a variant from a YAML model
docs.text:
Use the variant: field of the component you are configuring. If a component does not declare a variant, Trano falls back to the variant called default.

spaces:
  - id: SPACE:001
    parameters:
      floor_area: 80.0
      average_room_height: 2.5
    external_boundaries: ...
    emissions:
      - radiator:
          id: RADIATOR:001
          # Use the *ideal* radiator instead of the default detailed one
          variant: ideal
          parameters:
            nominal_heating_power_positive_for_heating: 2500
          control:
            emission_control:
              id: EMISSION_CONTROL:001
              # Use the on/off emission control variant
              variant: onoff
              parameters:
                schedule: 3600*{10, 20}
                temperature_heating_setpoint: 295.15
                temperature_heating_setback: 291.15

The variant key works the same way for any component in the YAML schema: spaces[i].variant, boiler.variant, air_handling_unit.variant, vav.variant, occupancy.variant, etc.

docs.title: 3. Creating a new variant
docs.text:
Creating a new variant is a small, focused YAML edit. There are two equally valid options:

Option When to use A — built-in variant The variant should ship with Trano and be available to everyone. B — external variants folder The variant is project- or vendor-specific; lives in your repo.

In both cases the YAML schema is identical.

docs.title: Step-by-step
docs.text:
1. Pick the class you want to extend (e.g. Radiator).
  2. Pick a unique variant name for that class. The name + library combo must be unique. The string is what users will write under variant: in their YAML model.
  3. Write the Modelica template as a Jinja2 string. Trano renders it with the element, package_name, library_name and parameters variables (see the existing templates under trano/elements/library/models/ for reference).
  4. Declare the ports — for hydronic components typically port_a / port_b fluid ports, plus optional heat ports (heatPortCon, heatPortRad) and data ports for control buses. The declared ports are also how Trano classifies the component when validating the model: a radiator variant with fluid ports is a water radiator (and must be followed by a valve); one without fluid ports needs no hydronic loop.
  5. Choose a parameter_processing function — default_parameters, modify_alias, exclude_parameters (see trano/elements/library/parameters.py).
  6. Save the file.

Below is the YAML you need to add a custom radiator that injects a fixed heat flow, driven by its control (same shape as the built-in ideal variant):

- classes:
  - Radiator
  variant: my_constant_emission
  library: default
  parameter_processing:
    function: default_parameters
  ports:
    - flow: convective
      medium: heat
      names: [heatPortCon]
      targets: [Space]
    - flow: radiative
      medium: heat
      names: [heatPortRad]
      targets: [Space]
    - flow: undirected
      medium: data
      names: [y]
      targets: [Control]
  template: |2-

      MyCompany.Trano.Emission.ConstantHeatRadiator
      {{ element.name }}(
        {{ macros.render_parameters(parameters) | safe }})
        "Constant-power radiator"
  figures: []

docs.title: Option A — Add the variant to Trano's built-in catalogue
docs.text:
Drop the YAML snippet above (as a list) into the right file under trano/elements/library/models/<library>/. For a radiator targeting every library, append it to trano/elements/library/models/default/radiator.yaml.

Built-in variants are also validated against the schema enums in trano/data_models/trano.yaml (e.g. RadiatorVariant), so a new built-in variant must be added there (and in trano_final.yaml) as well.

docs.title: Option B — Keep the variant in an external folder
docs.text:
If your variant should not live inside Trano (proprietary code, project specific, internal Modelica library...), place it in any folder of your choice and tell Trano about it.

my_project/
├── modelica/
│   └── MyCompany/...
└── trano_variants/             ← any path, anywhere
    └── radiator_constant.yaml  ← contains the YAML list shown above

There are three equivalent ways to register the folder:

docs.title: From the Python API
docs.text:
from trano.elements.library.components import register_variants_folder
from trano.main import create_model

register_variants_folder("my_project/trano_variants")
create_model("my_project/model.yaml")

register_variants_folder accepts str and pathlib.Path. The folder is scanned recursively for *.yaml files, so you can organise variants into sub-folders.

docs.title: From the CLI
docs.text:
trano create-model my_project/model.yaml --variants-folder my_project/trano_variants
trano simulate-model my_project/model.yaml --variants-folder my_project/trano_variants
trano compile-model my_project/model.yaml --variants-folder my_project/trano_variants

The --variants-folder option (-V) can be passed multiple times to register several folders.

docs.title: From an environment variable
docs.text:
export TRANO_VARIANTS_PATH="$HOME/my_project/trano_variants:$HOME/shared_variants"

Trano reads TRANO_VARIANTS_PATH whenever the component registry is loaded. The value is an os.pathsep-separated list of folders (: on Linux/macOS, ; on Windows).

docs.title: Using the new variant
docs.text:
Once registered, your variant is just like any built-in one — reference it by name:

emissions:
  - radiator:
      id: RADIATOR:001
      variant: my_constant_emission
      parameters:
        nominal_heating_power_positive_for_heating: 1500
      control:
        emission_control:
          id: EMISSION_CONTROL:001

docs.title: 4. Variants and model validation
docs.text:
Trano validates every model before generating it: against the schema (unknown fields, enums, bounds) and against topology rules (water loops, valves, controls). Externally registered variants take part in both:

  • The schema's variant enums only know the built-in variants; a variant: value that names a registered external variant of that component is accepted.
  • A radiator variant is classified by its declared ports: with fluid ports it is a water radiator and the usual rule applies (it must be followed by a valve in the emissions of its space); without fluid ports it is treated like the ideal variants and needs no hydronic loop.

An unknown variant (not built-in, not registered) is still rejected with the usual one-line validation error.

docs.title: 5. Programmatic listing and inspection
docs.text:
from trano.elements.library.components import (
    get_components_registry,
    register_variants_folder,
    registered_variants_folders,
    clear_variants_folders,
)

register_variants_folder("./trano_variants")

# What folders are currently registered?
print(registered_variants_folders())

# All variants known to Trano (built-in + external)
for c in get_components_registry().components:
    if "Radiator" in c["classes"]:
        print(c["library"], c["variant"])

# Reset to the built-in catalogue (useful in tests)
clear_variants_folders()

docs.title: 6. Testing your custom variant
docs.text:
A custom variant is just YAML, but it is still good practice to test it end-to-end. The recommended pattern:

from pathlib import Path

import pytest

from trano.elements.library.components import (
    clear_variants_folders,
    register_variants_folder,
)
from trano.elements.system import Radiator


@pytest.fixture(autouse=True)
def reset_variants():
    clear_variants_folders()
    yield
    clear_variants_folders()


def test_my_variant_is_registered(tmp_path: Path):
    register_variants_folder(Path(__file__).parent / "trano_variants")
    radiator = Radiator(name="r1", variant="my_constant_emission")
    library_data = next(ld for ld in radiator.libraries_data
                         if ld.variant == "my_constant_emission")
    assert "ConstantHeatRadiator" in library_data.template

For an end-to-end test that builds a network and a Modelica model from a YAML file, see tests/test_variants.py::test_create_model_yaml_using_custom_variant.

docs.title: 7. Cheat sheet
docs.text:
I want to ... Do this Use an existing variant Set variant: <name> on the component in your YAML model. Add a new variant for everyone Edit trano/elements/library/models/<library>/<component>.yaml and the variant enums in trano/data_models/trano.yaml / trano_final.yaml. Add a new variant only for my project Put YAML files in a folder, then register_variants_folder(folder). Register variants without changing my Python code export TRANO_VARIANTS_PATH=/path/to/folder. Register variants from the CLI trano create-model model.yaml --variants-folder /path/to/folder (also on simulate-model and compile-model). List registered external folders registered_variants_folders(). Reset to built-in only clear_variants_folders().

That's it — variants are the central extension point of Trano. Any new modelling capability (a new emission technology, a new control law, a new zone model from your in-house Modelica library...) is just a new YAML file.

docs.title: FastModel: models close to Buildings, in closed loop and for MPC
docs.text:
The FastModel library turns a YAML file into a model close to the Buildings library that still translates into a CasADi ODE (with rumoca) for simulation, state estimation and model predictive control with IPOPT:

  • every zone has the physics of Buildings.ThermalZones.Detailed.MixedAir: layered walls, floors and roofs, windows with the angular optics of their glazing, interior and exterior convection, long-wave exchange with the sky and between the room surfaces, the transmitted solar radiation distributed on the room surfaces, infiltration, walls and floors shared between zones;
  • the hydronic circuits of the YAML are modelled: radiators (EN 442), valves, mixing three-way valves, split valves, pumps, sensors, gas boilers and air-to-water heat pumps with their buffer;
  • balanced ventilation units with heat recovery (trano's system_d) and PV arrays.

The library has two configurations, built from the same components and templates:

  • FastModel simulates the building in closed loop, as the Buildings and IDEAS models do: the controllers of the YAML are part of the model (written without events) and the water flows follow the pressures of the circuits;
  • FastModelMPC is the model for optimal control: the controllers are left out, the controls of the systems are inputs that the optimisation decides, and each valve sets the flow of its branch.
trano create-model house.yaml FastModel       # closed loop: writes house.mo
trano simulate-model house.yaml FastModel     # runnable, like the other libraries
trano create-model house.yaml FastModelMPC    # the controls as inputs, for optimal control

docs.title: A library like Buildings and IDEAS
docs.text:
FastModel is used exactly as trano uses Buildings and IDEAS: a Modelica library and one template per element of the YAML, without code of its own.

  • trano/library/FastModel.mo holds the components (the physics), embedded in every generated package;
  • trano/elements/library/models/fast_model/*.yaml hold the templates that declare a component for each element of the YAML, with its ports, as the templates of the other libraries;
  • the FastModel entry of library.json writes the constructions and glazings as records of a Data package, takes the parameter names of Buildings, and the package template templates/fast_model.jinja2; the FastModelMPC entry extends it under another name, and the templates render each element for the library they are given (library == 'FastModel': controllers and pressure-driven circuits; 'FastModelMPC': inputs).

The walls, windows and floors are elements of their own connected to the bus of their zone, as in IDEAS: each OuterWall, Window, BoundaryWall (floor on ground or over outdoor air), AdiabaticWall or InternalWall connects its propsBus_a to a propsBus[i] of its Zone. The bus carries the convective and radiative exchanges with the room, the properties of the surface that the zone needs (area, emissivity, solar absorptance and transmittance), the solar radiation a window transmits, and the weather.

Package Components BoundaryConditions Weather (solar position and Perez sky of the site), TiltedSurface (irradiance on a surface) Envelope OuterWall, Window, BoundaryWall, AdiabaticWall, InternalWall Zones Zone, VentilatedZone Hydronics Radiator (EN 442), Valve, ThreeWayValve, Junction, Pump, TemperatureSensor, Boiler, HeatPump Ventilation HeatRecoveryUnit, Duct Electrical Photovoltaic HVAC IdealHeatingCooling (heat as an input), IdealHeater, IdealHeatingCoolingPI (closed loop) Controls EmissionP, EmissionPI, EmissionOnOff, EmissionMonitored, CollectorControl, ThreeWayValveControl, BoilerDemand, BoilerTemperatureControl, HeatPumpControl (closed loop, without events) Data Construction, Glazing (records written by trano)

The generated package holds two models:

  • building_mpc, the building: an explicit ODE whose inputs are the weather data, the internal gains and, with FastModelMPC, the controls of the systems. It contains no table, no event and no component of another library;
  • building, the runnable model: building_mpc fed with the weather file (the Buildings reader, which also gives building_mpc the location of the site), the occupancy schedules, and the external data of the network: the controls replayed from it with FastModelMPC (each held at 1 without data), the set points of the MonitoredSetpoint emission controls with FastModel.

Every component carries the icon of the Buildings model it follows (valves, pumps, radiators, boilers, heat pumps, walls, windows, zones, weather...), and its ports are placed on that icon, so that the model reads in a Modelica editor as a Buildings model does.

building_mpc is built as the Buildings and IDEAS models are, by the same code and configuration: its components are grouped in the containers of containers.yaml (envelope, emission, distribution, production, bus, ventilation, solar), which building_mpc extends as Components.Containers.building. The containers are linked by array ports (heatPortCon[n], port_a[n]...) of the FastModel connector types that library.json gives (connectors), and all share one data bus, dataBus. As with the other libraries, the components exchange their signals on the data bus: the data server of the bus container writes the air temperature of each zone, an emission control reads it and writes the opening of its valve, the collector control of the circuit reads the openings... and the systems outside the envelope read the weather there. A signal that no component writes is an input of building_mpc when its component says so (model_input in its YAML template: the weather data, the internal gains, the controls of FastModelMPC); the inputs are at the top of building_mpc, connected to the data bus. The data bus is the expandable connector of the other libraries with the signals of the network declared (data_bus_template), as rumoca does not add members to an expandable connector. The states carry the container in their names (envelope1.space_001.TAir). The containers do not change the equations; leave them out with network.model(include_container=False) or trano create-model house.yaml FastModel --no-containers for a single flat building_mpc.

docs.title: Rules for an explicit ODE
docs.text:
Every component keeps a few rules, so that rumoca translates the assembled model into xdot = f(t, x, u, p):

  • every node joined by connections has a heat capacity, or is solved in closed form inside its component (the radiant star of a room, the mixing of water flows);
  • the equations are smooth: power laws and table interpolations are regularised, conditions are inside functions; the controllers have no event (a hysteresis is a fast bistable state, a PI controller has anti-windup);
  • with FastModelMPC, flows are set: each valve sets the flow of its branch, a mixing valve the share of supply water, mass balances the rest; the production (boiler, heat pump) or the ventilation unit closes the balance of its circuit, one per circuit. With FastModel, they are pressure-driven: each component has a pressure node of small compliance at its inlet, every flow follows from the pressures, the pumps run on their curves;
  • a port with several connections is an array, one element per connection, sized by the template from the connections trano made: the inlets of a component mix, its outlets leave at its outlet temperature;
  • parameters computed by functions (the conductance of a radiator solved as Buildings does at initialisation, the polynomial fits of the window optics, the scaling of the heat pump tables) take values settled at translation.

docs.title: Inputs of building_mpc
docs.text:
The closed-loop FastModel takes the weather, the internal gains and, for a MonitoredSetpoint emission control, its set point <control>_TSet; FastModelMPC takes the controls too:

Input Role weather_inputs.TDryBul, .TBlaSky, .winSpe, .winDir, .HDirNor, .HDifHor, .HGloHor weather data, as in a weather file or a forecast (disturbances) <occupancy>_gai.QCon, .QRad convective and radiant internal gains per floor area [W/m2] (disturbances) <valve>_y.y flow of a radiator branch relative to its nominal flow (control, 0 to 1) <three-way valve>_y.y share of supply water (control) <boiler>_y.y boiler part load ratio, or heat pump compressor speed (control) <ventilation unit>_y.y air flow relative to the design flow (control held at 1 by its bounds, as Buildings runs it) <emitter>_Q.Q_flow heat of an ideal emitter [W] (control, between its bounds)

The solar position and the irradiance on each surface are computed inside the model from the time (the clock time of the year) and the site, so that a forecast only needs the weather channels. The meters of the systems are states in kWh: EFue (boiler fuel), EEle (heat pump electricity), EFan (fans), EPro (PV production).

docs.title: Simulation, estimation and optimal control: trano_optimization
docs.text:
The CasADi side lives in trano-optimization (trano_optimization), a package of its own that depends on rumoca, CasADi, NumPy and pydantic only, not on trano; install it next to trano (pip install trano-optimization). It reads everything from the Modelica model: the names of the states, inputs and parameters in the order of the CasADi vectors, their units, bounds and descriptions. The roles of the variables follow simple conventions (Roles.infer): an input with a min and a max is a control, any other input a disturbance; the states named TAir are the comfort temperatures; the states in kWh are meters.

from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np

from trano.data_models.conversion import convert_network
from trano.elements.library.library import Library
from trano_optimization import KELVIN, CasadiModel, OptimalControl, OptimalControlSettings

network = convert_network("house", Path("house.yaml"), library=Library.from_configuration("FastModelMPC"))
model = CasadiModel.from_modelica(network.model(), "house.building_mpc")
ocp = OptimalControl(model, settings=OptimalControlSettings(time_step=3600))

hours = np.arange(24)
comfort = np.where((hours >= 7) & (hours < 22), KELVIN + 20, KELVIN + 16)
disturbances = ...  # (len(ocp.roles.disturbances), 24): forecasts of the weather and gains
result = ocp.solve(model.description.initial_state, disturbances, comfort, price=np.full(24, 0.10),
                   start_time=t0)  # the model time of the first step: the solar position depends on it
result.controls  # branch flows, valve positions, boiler part load ratio, hour by hour

OptimalControl collocates the ODE on Radau points (stable for the stiff water nodes whatever the step), solves with IPOPT (SPRAL when CasADi ships it, MUMPS otherwise), warm-starts from a simulation of the model (CVODES), and costs the energy read from the meters: the PV production first covers the electricity of the step, the rest is sold at feed_in_price; the boiler fuel has its own fuel_price. The same discretization gives the moving horizon estimation and the closed loop:

from trano_optimization import MovingHorizonEstimation, receding_horizon

estimator = MovingHorizonEstimation(model)
estimate = estimator.estimate(prior_state, applied_controls, past_disturbances, measured_air_temperatures)
loop = receding_horizon(ocp, estimate.current, disturbances, comfort, price, horizon=12, start_time=t0)

The parameters computed from others (a conductance from a thickness and a conductivity) are parameters of their own in the CasADi function, at their values: an identification adjusts the effective ones (conductances, capacities).

docs.title: How close to Buildings
docs.text: python -m validation.mpc simulates the Buildings model of a YAML file and compares it with FastModel in two ways: it replays what the systems of Buildings did (the heat of ideal emitters, or the branch flows, valve positions and boiler or heat pump controls) through the runnable FastModelMPC model (--models FastModel), or it simulates the closed-loop FastModel with its own controllers (--models FastModelClosedLoop); then it compares the zones, the water temperatures and the meters. See the validation page for the results.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• One production (boiler or heat pump) per hydraulic circuit, and mixing three-way valves (the bypass from the return): diverting valves are not modelled yet.
  • Ventilation units are balanced (supply = extract) and of the system_d kind.
  • Boilers with a storage tank, water-to-water heat pumps, chillers, domestic hot water, batteries, EV chargers and VAV systems are not modelled: generating a model with them stops with a message naming them.
  • With FastModelMPC, flows are set by the valves; the pressure-driven sharing of flow between branches is modelled in the closed loop only, with the resistances linearised at their nominal flows.
  • The closed-loop controllers have no event: a hysteresis switches within 10 s, and the minimum on and off times of the heat pump are not modelled.

docs.title: First model and simulation
docs.text: This tutorial will guide you in creating and simulating your first Building Energy Simulation model in Modelica using the Trano library. All you need is a configuration file and a few lines of code. This introductory tutorial demonstrates the simplicity of running building energy simulations with Trano, showcasing how to browse and modify the model using OpenModelica. Alternatively, you can run the simulation directly through Trano with the official OpenModelica Docker image. Additionally, Trano features automatic report generation for key parameters.

docs.title: Input configuration file
docs.text:
The following file describes a single-zone house: 100 m2 of floor (12.5 m by 8 m, 2.5 m high) with a large south-facing window and a small north one, brick and insulation walls, an insulated flat roof and a slab on the ground. The house is occupied in the morning and in the evening, infiltrates 0.5 air changes per hour, and an ideal heating and cooling system keeps it between a heating set point of 21 degC by day (18 degC at night) and a cooling set point of 26 degC.

A few conventions of the file:

  • Materials and constructions: a construction is a list of layers from the outside to the inside, each layer being a material and a thickness. The glazing is described the same way with glass panes and gas gaps, and trano computes the U-value and the g-value of the glazing from its layers.
  • Orientation: azimuths are in radians, 0 being south, positive towards the west (1.5708 is west, 3.1416 north, -1.5708 east). A wall's surface is the gross area of the facade: the windows facing the same way are cut out of it, so the window area must not be subtracted from the wall. The flat roof is an external wall with the ceiling tilt.
  • Zone: the infiltration variant takes the air change rate ach; the occupancy table lists the times at which the zone switches between occupied and unoccupied (7:00 to 9:00 and 18:00 to 23:00 here); the ideal system takes day schedules of set points in kelvin (rows of time since midnight in seconds and set point) and its capacities.

Every parameter is optional: a parameter left out takes the default of the library the model is generated for (see the parameter reference).

docs.title: Hydronic heating with mixing circuits
docs.text: This tutorial heats the three zones of the hydronic heating tutorial with a hydronic system wired the way a heating engineer would wire it: each group of radiators has a mixing circuit with its pump after its three-way valve. The boiler can then run hot while the radiators get the water temperature they are designed for.

docs.title: Why the pump goes after the three-way valve
docs.text:
A three-way valve controlled on temperature has to mix: it blends the hot water of the boiler (port_1) with the cooler water coming back from the radiators (port_3) and sends the blend to the radiators (port_2). Its controller measures the temperature after the valve and opens or closes the valve to hold it at a set point.

Mixing only happens if something pulls the return water into port_3: the pump of the circuit, placed after the valve.

boiler ──► port_1 ┐
                  ├ THREE-WAY VALVE ── port_2 ──► sensor ──► pump ──► radiators ──► radiator valves
          port_3 ─┘                                                                       │
            ▲                                                                             ▼
            └──────────────────────────────── split valve ◄───────────────────────────────┘
                                                   │
                                                   └──► back to the boiler

When the pump is placed before the valve, as in the earlier hydronic tutorials, it pushes the water into port_1: the water then leaves through port_3 back to the boiler instead of being drawn in. The valve no longer mixes, it diverts: closing it sends hot water back to the boiler instead of to the radiators, but the water that does reach the radiators is still as hot as the boiler supply. The valve can cut the flow, never lower the temperature. If the boiler supply exceeds the set point of the valve, the controller closes the valve completely and the rooms go cold: with the default boiler set point of 80 degC, the top of the storage tank reaches about 95 degC, above the default 90 degC of the valve, and the rooms of such a model fell to 16 degC. Trano reports that layout with a HydronicLayoutWarning (see the note in the hydronic heating tutorial).

docs.title: Configuration of the systems
docs.text:
The envelope, the occupancy and the emissions are those of the hydronic heating tutorial; only the systems change. Each mixing circuit is a chain three_way_valve -> temperature_sensor -> pump -> radiators:

  • the boiler feeds the three-way valves directly (outlets of the boiler);
  • the three-way valve lists the split valve of its circuit in its inlets: that is the return water mixed in through port_3. Its control holds supply_temperature_setpoint (70 degC here; 90 degC when absent) with a PI controller (see below);
  • the temperature sensor comes right after the valve: its control measures the mixed water there;
  • the pump comes after the sensor and feeds the radiators of the circuit. Each circuit has its own pump; a single pump before several valves cannot make them mix;
  • the split valve collects the return of the radiator valves and sends it to the boiler; the three-way valve draws its share of it.

docs.title: Tuning the valve controller
docs.text:
three_way_valve_control takes the parameters of its controller (controller_type, k, ti, ...; see the parameters). This example uses a PI controller with a gain of 0.1 per kelvin and an integral time of 300 s; the lessons learned at the end of this page explain why.

The model is created as in the other tutorials:

Test three zones hydronic mixing

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Two January weeks simulated with IDEAS. The rooms are heated to 21 degC from 7 to 19 h and fall back to 16 degC at night; the boiler, with its default 80 degC set point, charges its storage tank up to about 95 degC.

The figure below shows the mixing at work. While the top of the tank is above 75 degC (it rises to 94 degC), the water sent to the radiators stays at the 70 degC set point of the valves (median 70.0 degC; 95 % of the time below 76 degC; it dips when the rooms start heating after the night setback and the valves open fully). The rooms average 20.3 to 20.5 degC during the occupied hours. With the pump before the valves, that water would follow the tank temperature.

docs.title: Lessons learned: the PID of the three-way valves
docs.text:
These lessons come from simulating three January days of this model with IDEAS, changing only the controller of the two valves. The figures are for the water sent to the radiators while the top of the tank is above 75 degC.

Controller of the valves Water to the radiators: median 95 % of the time below Rooms (occupied, mean) Time to simulate Default: proportional, k = 1 per K 68 to 69 degC 75 degC 20.3 to 20.4 degC 451 s Proportional, k = 0.1 per K 63 degC 71 degC 20.2 to 20.3 degC 128 s PI, k = 0.1 per K, ti = 300 s 70.0 degC 76 degC 20.3 to 20.4 degC 110 s Pump before the valves (earlier tutorial), default controller follows the tank — — 25 s

1. The tuning only matters once the valve really regulates. With the pump before the valves, the valves sit fully open, the controller never acts, and the default tuning looks fine: that model simulates in 25 s. The same controller on valves that do mix made the simulation 18 times slower. A layout that works hides the weaknesses of its controls, so a model only tells you about its controller once the controller has something to do.

2. The gain has units, and 1 per kelvin is a lot for a valve. The controller turns a temperature error in kelvin into a valve opening between 0 and 1. With k = 1, an error of 1 K already moves the valve over its whole stroke. Between the valve and the sensor there are delays: the mixing volume, the sensor's time constant, the travel of the water and, in IDEAS, the actuator of the valve. A large gain acting through delays overshoots, corrects and overshoots again: the valve hunts around the set point, and every reversal is a fast change the solver follows with small steps. We did not record the valve finely enough to see each reversal, but the timings point to it: lowering the gain alone cut the simulation from 451 s to 128 s.

3. A proportional controller cannot reach its set point. It only opens the valve in proportion to the error, so it needs a permanent error to hold the valve open: the opening divided by k. With k = 1 and the valves about 70 % open, that offset is 0.7 K (68 to 69 degC for a 70 degC set point), which is why it goes unnoticed. Lowering the gain to calm the valve makes the offset ten times larger: k = 0.1 held the water at 63 degC, 7 K below the set point. A proportional controller makes you choose between a calm valve and an accurate temperature.

4. The integral action removes that choice. A PI controller keeps adding up the error, so it holds the set point with a small gain: 70.0 degC with k = 0.1, in 110 s. Its integral time must be slow compared with the delays of the circuit (mixing volume, sensor, valve actuator): 300 s here.

5. Never switch to PI without setting ti. The default ti is 0.5 s. It is unused by the proportional controller, but it becomes active as soon as controller_type is set to PI. An integral time of half a second is far faster than the delays of the circuit, a classic cause of oscillation (we did not simulate it). Always give controller_type, k and ti together.

6. How to check a tuning. Plot the valve opening and the temperature after the valve (as in the second figure of the results):

  • the opening zig-zags, or the simulation is unusually slow: the gain is too high, lower k;
  • the temperature settles away from the set point: there is no integral action, use PI;
  • the temperature drifts slowly back and forth around the set point: the integral is too fast, raise ti.

The PI values of this example are a starting point that worked here. We tested only the three tunings above, so check them on your own circuit with the plots above rather than reusing them blindly. The default of three_way_valve_control is still the proportional controller, so that the existing models keep their results.

docs.text: Switching libraries is seamless with Trano. This tutorial demonstrates how to generate a model using the IDEAS library from the same YAML file previously utilized.

docs.title: Supported libraries
docs.text: The same YAML file generates a model for each of the libraries trano supports: Buildings (13.0.0) and IDEAS (3.0.0) for detailed zones, reduced_order (the AixLib 3.0.1 reduced-order zone) and iso_13790 (the ISO 13790 zone of AixLib) for simplified zones, and FastModel (closed loop) or FastModelMPC (for optimal control) for models close to Buildings that translate to CasADi (see the FastModel reference). Buildings and IDEAS are validated against ASHRAE Standard 140 (BESTEST), see the validation results and the walk through the cases; the simplified zones are reported there for information. The parameter reference lists, for every parameter, the Modelica name it is rendered under in each library and the parameters a library does not take.

docs.title: Zone template (IDEAS only)
docs.text:
By default Trano renders an IDEAS envelope with separate components: an IDEAS.Buildings.Components.Zone plus one OuterWall, Window or SlabOnGround array per construction. IDEAS also provides IDEAS.Buildings.Components.RectangularZoneTemplate, a single component bundling the zone, its four vertical faces, floor and ceiling. Set the space variant to rectangular_zone to use it:

spaces:
  - id: SPACE:001
    variant: rectangular_zone
    parameters:
      floor_area: 80.0
      average_room_height: 2.5
    external_boundaries:
      external_walls:
        - surface: 90.0
          azimuth: 3.14
          tilt: wall
          construction: CONSTRUCTION:001
      floor_on_grounds:
        - surface: 80.0
          construction: CONSTRUCTION:001
      windows:
        - surface: 1.5
          azimuth: 3.14
          tilt: wall
          construction: INS2AR2020:001

Trano maps the walls onto the four faces of the template (face A takes the orientation shared by most surfaces, the other faces are at 90° steps from it), lumps the windows of a face sharing a glazing into one window, and uses the floor on ground as SlabOnGround and a horizontal roof as the ceiling. Surfaces that do not fit the rectangle (pitched roofs, a second construction or glazing on the same face, extra orientations) and the internal walls stay separate components connected through the template's proBusExt bus, so nothing is lost. The variant is only available with the IDEAS library.

docs.title: Multi-zone with hydronic heating
docs.text:
The previous tutorials provided idealized examples. In this tutorial, we will simulate a three-zone building with a hydronic heating system, aiming for a more realistic model. Below, we will describe the configuration file, highlighting key points:

  • Default Construction Values: Trano includes a set of predefined construction, glazing, and gas properties. To use these in your configuration file, add the following line: 

    default: !include_default

  • Emission Systems: Each space is assigned a list of emission systems. These are linked to a radiator object (RADIATOR:001) and a valve object (VALVE:001), with the valve being used for control instead of the radiator: 

    emissions:
  - radiator:
      id: RADIATOR:001
  - valve:
      id: VALVE:001
      control:
        emission_control:

  • Hydronic System Definition: A complete hydronic system must be defined, including the boiler, pump, and various valves. Default parameters will be utilized if not specified:

  - boiler:
      id: BOILER:001
      control:
        boiler_control:
  - pump:
      id: PUMP:001
      control:
        collector_control:
      outlets:
        - THREE_WAY_VALVE:001
        - THREE_WAY_VALVE:002
      inlets:
        - BOILER:001

      id: SPLIT_VALVE:001
      inlets:
        - VALVE:003

      outlets:

docs.title: Why the layout of this tutorial is wrong
docs.text:
The pump of this tutorial is before the three-way valves

This tutorial wires the hydronic system as boiler -> pump -> three-way valves -> sensors -> radiators. That layout does not work as a supply temperature control, and Trano reports it with a HydronicLayoutWarning ("WRONG HYDRONIC LAYOUT") on each three-way valve. It is kept as it is so that existing models keep working; build new models as in Hydronic heating with mixing circuits.

What the three-way valves are meant to do. Each valve has a controller that measures the water after the valve (TEMPERATURE_SENSOR) and should hold it at a set point, 90 degC by default, by mixing the hot water of the boiler with the cooler return water of the radiators.

What they do here. The pump pushes the water into port_1 of the valves. The water inside a valve is then at a higher pressure than the return, so port_3 sends water back to the boiler instead of drawing return water in. Closing the valve diverts hot water to the return; the water that still reaches the radiators is as hot as the boiler supply. The valve can reduce the flow to the radiators, never lower their temperature.

What goes wrong. The boiler charges its storage tank until the bottom of the tank is 5 K above tsup_nominal, so the top of the tank, which feeds the radiators, ends about 15 K above it: about 95 degC with the default 80 degC. Above the 90 degC set point, the controller closes the valve to cool the water; that does not cool it, so it keeps closing until the valve is shut. Almost no water reaches the radiators, the sensor sits in still hot water and keeps reading "too hot", and the valve never reopens. In simulation, the rooms of tests/models/three_zones_hydronic.yaml averaged 16 degC instead of 21 degC. This tutorial avoids it only because its boiler is set to 70 degC (tsup_nominal: 343.15): the tank stays below 90 degC, the valves stay fully open and in fact control nothing.

The workaround Trano applies. When the supply of a storage boiler can exceed the set point of such a valve, Trano raises the set point of the valve 5 K above the expected top of the tank (100 degC for the default 80 degC boiler) and says so in the warning ("WORKAROUND APPLIED"). The valve then stays open and the rooms are heated again (21 degC in simulation), but the radiators receive the boiler water unmixed: nothing limits their supply temperature, the radiator valves alone control the rooms. To make it an error instead, filter the warning: warnings.simplefilter("error", HydronicLayoutWarning) (from trano.validation.issues).

The fix. Put one pump after each three-way valve and its sensor, and list the return split valve in the inlets of the valve: the pump then draws the return water into the valve, which mixes and holds its set point (supply_temperature_setpoint of three_way_valve_control) whatever the boiler supply. See Hydronic heating with mixing circuits.
